battle.title: Polymorphism Playground
battle.description: Same call, many behaviours: overriding, dispatch and overload traps.

questions.text: With  Animal a = new Dog();  a.speak();  what decides which version of speak() runs?
options: The declared type Animal, fixed at compile time
The actual object type Dog, decided at runtime
Whichever class appears first in the source file
The order in which the methods are written in Animal
questions.answer: The actual object type Dog, decided at runtime
questions.explanation: Overridden instance methods are dispatched on the real object at runtime. The declared type only decides which methods may be called, so thinking Animal's version always runs is the common mistake.
Dog overrides sound(), while Cat does not, so it inherits Animal's version and prints '...'. The base Animal object also prints '...'.
Methods are overridden and dispatched on the real object (C.who), but fields are not polymorphic: p.name uses the declared type P, so it is 'parent'. Expecting 'child' treats the field like a method.

questions.text: Your app must process Card, Cash and Wallet payments, and new payment types will be added later. Which design uses polymorphism best?
options: One pay() method with a long if-else chain on a type string
A Payment interface with pay(), one class per type, called through the interface
Separate unrelated classes and a separate loop for each type
A static method per type, chosen by a switch in main
questions.answer: A Payment interface with pay(), one class per type, called through the interface
questions.explanation: Callers just invoke pay() on a Payment and the right code runs, so a new type needs no change to existing code. The if-else or switch versions must be edited every time a type is added.

Overloads are chosen at compile time from the declared argument type. The variable o is declared Object, so f(Object) runs even though it holds a String; the literal "hi" is a String. Overloading is not runtime polymorphism.

coding.title: Payroll Polymorphism
coding.description: Read n employees, one per line. Kinds: FULL s (pay = s + s/10), PART h r (pay = h*r, plus ((h-40)*r)/2 extra if h > 40), CONTRACT d r (pay = d*r), INTERN (pay = 500). All divisions are integer divisions. Model them with an abstract class and subclasses, print each employee's pay on its own line, then a final line TOTAL followed by the sum.
coding.inputDescription: Line 1: n. Next n lines: an employee record as described.
coding.outputDescription: n lines with each pay, then one line 'TOTAL x'.
coding.constraints: 1 <= n <= 1000, all numbers are non-negative and at most 100000

debug.title: The Ticket That Never Upgrades
debug.description: Each order is a type (B for basic, P for premium) and a quantity. Basic tickets cost 10 each and premium tickets cost 15 each. The program should print the total cost, but premium orders are charged the basic price. Input: n, then n lines 'type qty'. Output: the total.
hints: Try a single premium order, P 1. What total do you expect and what do you get?
Premium has its own cost method, yet the basic price is being used. Compare the two cost method headers.
One method takes int and the other takes long. Are they really the same method signature?
A method only overrides when its signature matches exactly. Change Premium.cost to take int qty (and add @Override so the compiler checks it).
